questions.q: In the complex CoCl₃·5NH₃, 1 mol of the compound gives 2 mol of AgCl with excess AgNO₃. What is the correct formula?
questions.explain: 2 mol of Cl⁻ are free (outside), so one Cl is inside the complex ion. The coordination number is 6 (5 NH₃ + 1 Cl).

questions.q: According to Werner's theory, the secondary valency is equal to the metal's:
questions.explain: The secondary valency is non-ionisable and equals the coordination number; the primary valency equals the oxidation number.

questions.q: What are the oxidation number and coordination number of Fe in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻?
questions.explain: Charge = x + 6(−1) = −4, so x = +2. Six unidentate CN⁻ give coordination number 6.

questions.q: Which of the following is a didentate ligand?
questions.explain: en has two nitrogen donor atoms and can form two bonds. The others are unidentate.

questions.q: What is the coordination number in [Co(en)₃]³⁺?
What is the IUPAC name of K₃[Fe(CN)₆]?
questions.explain: K₃ means the complex ion has charge 3−; x − 6 = −3, so Fe is +3. Because the complex is an anion, iron is called ferrate.

questions.q: In which order are the ligands named in [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)Cl]Cl₂?
questions.explain: Alphabetically ammine < aqua < chlorido; multiplying prefixes such as tetra are ignored.

questions.q: How many geometrical isomers are possible for square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]?
questions.explain: cis and trans: two in total.

questions.q: Which of the following shows optical isomerism?
questions.explain: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ is octahedral and its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it (it is chiral). The trans form has a plane of symmetry, and [Ni(CO)₄] and [PtCl₄]²⁻ are symmetric.

questions.q: What kind of isomerism exists between [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]SO₄ and [Co(NH₃)₅SO₄]Cl?
questions.explain: The counter ion (SO₄²⁻ / Cl⁻) and a ligand have been exchanged: ionisation isomerism.

questions.q: According to VBT, what are the hybridisations of [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and [CoF₆]³⁻?
questions.explain: NH₃ is a strong-field ligand: the 3d electrons pair up and the complex is d²sp³ (inner orbital, diamagnetic). F⁻ is a weak-field ligand: 4d is used, giving sp³d² (outer orbital, 4 unpaired electrons).

questions.q: What are the geometry and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and [NiCl₄]²⁻?
options: square planar, diamagnetic and tetrahedral, paramagnetic
tetrahedral, diamagnetic and square planar, paramagnetic
questions.explain: CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand: dsp², square planar, no unpaired electrons. Cl⁻ is a weak-field ligand: sp³, tetrahedral, two unpaired electrons.

questions.q: In an octahedral field with Δ₀ > P, what are the configuration and the number of unpaired electrons of a d⁶ ion?
questions.explain: Δ₀ > P gives low spin: all the electrons pair up in t₂g, so t₂g⁶ e_g⁰ with 0 unpaired.

options: The d electron in t₂g absorbs blue-green light and is promoted to e_g (a d–d transition)
questions.explain: Ti³⁺ is d¹. It absorbs at 498 nm (blue-green), so the complementary colour, violet, is seen.

questions.q: What are the oxidation state and geometry of Ni in [Ni(CO)₄]?
questions.explain: CO is neutral, so Ni is 0; sp³ hybridisation, tetrahedral, diamagnetic (3d¹⁰).

questions.q: Why can EDTA be used to determine the hardness of water?
options: It forms stable complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, with different stability constants
questions.explain: Titration with Na₂EDTA lets Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ be estimated separately.
